note: Drafted by the chat assistant 11-04 for the owner's review (D150 T03b, third wider-CS batch). Nothing is live until approved in Admin → Learn → Questions. 'pieces' are suggested Learn step ids to verify (empty where no Learn piece fits yet).

items.stem: After your latest release, the app crashes on launch for some users. Crash reports show a field from the API is missing for older accounts. What do you do?
choices: Treat the field as optional with a safe default, add a test using an old account's response, and ship the fix through a staged rollout
Wrap app launch in a try/catch that ignores errors
Pull the release from the store so the crash goes away
Ask affected users to reinstall the app
why: Handling the missing field fixes the cause, the test stops it coming back, and a staged rollout limits the damage if anything else is wrong.
The app starts in a broken state, and the next problem is hidden too.
Copies already installed keep crashing; unlike a server, you can't roll back an app on people's phones.
Reinstalling gets the same version and the same crash.

items.stem: Scrolling a feed of photos stutters on older Android phones. What's the fix?
choices: Load images sized for the view, cache them, and decode them off the main thread
Preload every image when the app starts
Show a loading spinner over the feed while it scrolls
Turn off all animations
why: Smaller images mean less work, caching avoids repeating it, and decoding off the main thread keeps scrolling smooth.
Uses far more memory and slows the launch.
Hides the feed without reducing the work.
The stutter comes from image work, not animations.

items.stem: Users writing posts on the subway lose their drafts when the connection drops. What do you build?
choices: Disable editing while offline
Keep the draft in memory until it's sent
Save drafts to local storage as they type, queue the changes, and sync when the connection returns, handling any conflicts
Show an error and ask them to try again later
why: Users can't do anything on the subway.
Lost if the app is closed or killed.
Local-first saving means nothing is lost, and syncing later makes the connection drop invisible.
The draft is still lost.

items.stem: You're releasing a risky new feature on mobile, where you can't instantly undo a release. How do you ship it?
choices: Release to everyone, and send a hotfix if it breaks
Keep it in a closed beta for months
Behind a server-controlled feature flag with a staged rollout, watching the crash-free rate, with a kill switch
Release it on one platform only
why: Store review and slow updates mean a hotfix can take days to reach people.
Feedback comes late, and real-world problems still appear at launch.
The flag lets you turn the feature off without a new release, and the staged rollout limits who sees problems first.
Half your users still get the risk, with no way to switch it off.

items.stem: Old versions of your app are still in use, and you need to change an API they depend on. What do you do?
choices: Keep the old API working alongside the new one, measure which app versions are still active, and only for truly breaking changes set a minimum version with an update prompt
Keep every API version running forever
Email users asking them to update
Change the API; people should update
why: Backward compatibility protects users, data on active versions tells you when it's safe to retire the old path, and a minimum version is the last resort.
The maintenance cost grows without end.
Few people act on it, and the app still breaks for the rest.
Users on old versions find the app broken.

items.stem: Users complain about battery drain. The app checks the server every 30 seconds in the background. What do you change?
choices: Use push notifications for updates, and the platform's background scheduler for any work that must run, batched together
Ask users to close the app when they're not using it
Run an always-on background service
Check every 60 seconds instead
why: The device wakes only when there's something new, and the scheduler groups work at efficient times.
Users won't, and they shouldn't have to.
Drains the battery more, and the platform may kill it anyway.
Half the drain, same design.

items.stem: A counter is incremented in an interrupt handler and read in the main loop. On your 8-bit microcontroller, the main loop sometimes reads a wildly wrong value. What's the fix?
choices: Add a short delay before reading it
Declare it volatile, and read it with interrupts briefly disabled (or with an atomic access), because a multi-byte value can change halfway through the read
Increase the clock speed
Read it twice and average the results
why: The interrupt can still fire mid-read.
volatile stops the compiler caching it, and protecting the read stops the interrupt splitting a multi-byte value.
Faster code still races with the interrupt.
Averaging two torn values is still wrong.

items.stem: Devices in the field occasionally freeze, and you can't reproduce it in the lab. What do you do?
choices: Add more debug prints to the lab build
Ask customers to power-cycle the device when it freezes
Add a watchdog that resets the device if it stops responding, record the reset reason and last state in persistent storage, and use those reports to find the cause
Double the size of every buffer
why: The lab can't reproduce it, so the prints never show it.
Customers carry the cost, and you learn nothing.
The watchdog recovers on its own, and the stored reports give you evidence from the field, where the bug actually happens.
A guess that may hide the bug, or not touch it.

items.stem: A device that runs for months calls malloc and free constantly. After a few weeks, allocations start failing even though total free memory looks fine. What's going on, and what's the fix?
choices: Add a garbage collector
Heap fragmentation: use static allocation or fixed-size memory pools on the long-running paths
Schedule a weekly reboot
Make the heap bigger
why: Adds unpredictable pauses and doesn't remove fragmentation.
Free memory has been split into pieces too small to use; pools of fixed-size blocks can't fragment.
Hides the problem, and fails if anything delays the reboot.
Delays the failure without preventing it.

items.stem: You need to update firmware on 50,000 devices in the field. What makes the update safe?
choices: Download the image over plain HTTP to keep it simple
Overwrite the running firmware in place to save space
Ask customers to send devices back for updates
Signed images, two firmware slots (A/B), verify the new image before switching, and roll back automatically if it fails to boot
why: Anyone on the network could send their own firmware.
A power cut mid-update can leave a device unusable.
Expensive and slow, so few devices get updated.
Signatures stop tampered images, and two slots mean a failed update always falls back to working firmware.

items.stem: In your RTOS, a high-priority task sometimes misses its deadline while a low-priority task holds a shared mutex and a medium-priority task keeps running. What's happening, and what's the fix?
choices: Raise every task to high priority
Poll the mutex in a tight loop from the high-priority task
Give the high-priority task a longer deadline
Priority inversion: use a mutex with priority inheritance, and keep the locked sections short
why: Priorities stop meaning anything.
Wastes CPU and makes starvation worse.
Changes the requirement instead of fixing the system.
The low-priority holder is temporarily raised, so it finishes and releases the lock before the medium task can starve it.

items.stem: A logging service on an embedded Linux box uses a lot of CPU. Profiling shows most time goes to write() calls, one per log line. What do you change?
choices: Buffer log lines and write them in batches (or use buffered I/O)
Move to a faster CPU
Restart the service every hour
Lower the process priority
why: Fewer system calls means far less overhead for the same output.
More cost for the same wasteful pattern.
Doesn't change how it writes.
The work still happens, just later.

items.stem: The end-to-end test suite takes 90 minutes and blocks every merge. What do you change?
choices: Delete the end-to-end tests
Buy faster CI machines and change nothing else
Run tests only before a release
Move most checks into fast unit and integration tests, keep a small set of critical end-to-end journeys on every merge, run them in parallel, and run the full suite nightly
why: You lose the checks that catch problems across the whole system.
Helps a little; the suite is still too slow by design.
Bugs pile up and are found when they're hardest to fix.
Fast feedback on every merge, with the slow, broad checks still running every day.

items.stem: A test checks a "trial expires in 7 days" banner and fails whenever it runs near midnight. What's the fix?
choices: Only run the test at noon
Add a sleep until the date changes
Inject a clock (or freeze time in the test) so the test controls what "now" is
Mark it flaky and skip it
why: The test still depends on the real clock, and CI doesn't care what time it is.
Slow, and still timing-dependent.
When the test sets the time, it gives the same result whenever it runs.
You lose the check entirely.

items.stem: A support ticket says "checkout is broken sometimes." What turns it into something an engineer can fix?
choices: Close it as "cannot reproduce"
Reassign it to the checkout team as it is
Steps to reproduce, the environment (device, browser, account type), expected versus actual result, how often it happens, and the logs or request ids
Attach a screenshot and nothing else
why: The bug is real for the customer and stays unfixed.
Someone has to start from scratch.
With those details, an engineer can reproduce it and find the cause quickly.
Shows the symptom without how to get there.

items.stem: Tests pass on their own but fail when the whole suite runs, depending on the order. What's the fix?
choices: Reset the shared test database once a day
Isolate each test's data (factories or fixtures per test, with transactions rolled back or a fresh database), so no test depends on another's leftovers
Fix the run order so they always pass
Run every test one at a time
why: Tests still share state within each day.
Each test sets up what it needs and cleans up after itself, so order stops mattering.
Hides the dependency until someone adds a test.
Slow, and the shared-state bug is still there.

items.stem: You have limited time to automate testing for a large product. What do you automate first?
choices: Whatever is easiest to automate
Nothing until the product stops changing
Stable, high-risk, often-repeated checks (sign-in, checkout, the core flows), keeping exploratory testing for new features
Everything, through the UI, to reach 100% coverage
why: Easy isn't the same as valuable.
Products rarely stop changing; you'd never start.
Automation pays off most where failures cost the most and checks repeat often, and people explore what's new.
Slow, brittle tests that break with every design change.

items.stem: Two services keep breaking each other's integration after independent deploys. What do you add?
choices: Deploy both services together every time
Consumer-driven contract tests: each consumer publishes what it expects, and the provider's CI checks those expectations before it deploys
A full manual integration test once a week
Let each team mock the other service however it likes
why: Couples the teams and slows everyone down.
The provider learns before deploying that a change would break a consumer, and teams keep deploying independently.
Breakage is found up to a week late.
Mocks drift from reality, so tests pass while production breaks.

items.stem: A strong engineer's output has dropped, and they seem disengaged. What do you do first?
choices: Quietly move their work to someone else
Have a private one-to-one to listen and understand what's changed, then agree together what support or changes would help
Wait for the next performance review
Raise it in the team stand-up
why: They'll notice, and trust drops on both sides.
Most causes, such as workload, health, or a project that isn't working, only come out in a private conversation, and solving it together keeps their trust.
Months of a problem that a conversation might fix now.
Public, and likely to make things worse.

items.stem: Two senior engineers disagree about an architecture, and the team is blocked. What do you do?
choices: Build both and see which works
Go with the more senior engineer's view
Let them keep debating until they agree
Ask both to write down their options and trade-offs against criteria the team agrees on, decide within a set time, and ask everyone to commit, even those who disagree
why: Doubles the work and splits the team.
Seniority isn't a reason, and the other engineer disengages.
The team stays blocked.
Writing it down turns opinions into trade-offs, the time limit unblocks the team, and committing after disagreeing keeps everyone moving together.

items.stem: Your team keeps getting pulled into urgent requests and misses its goals every sprint. What do you change?
choices: Add a daily meeting to discuss interruptions
Refuse every unplanned request
Ask the team to work weekends to catch up
Make all requests visible, set up one intake path with a rotating person handling interruptions, and agree priorities with stakeholders
why: More time lost to the same problem.
Some urgent requests really are urgent.
Burns the team out and fixes nothing.
One visible path and a rotation protect the rest of the team's focus, and agreed priorities make trade-offs explicit.

items.stem: You need to hire three engineers quickly without lowering the bar. How do you run the process?
choices: Let each interviewer ask what they like and go with gut feel
Lower the bar for now and raise it later
Hire people the team already knows
Structured interviews with clear criteria, trained and calibrated interviewers, and written scorecards submitted before discussion
why: Inconsistent and prone to bias.
Hiring mistakes are slow and costly to undo.
Fast, but it narrows the team and skips real evaluation.
The same criteria for everyone makes decisions fairer and faster, and written scores before discussion stop the loudest voice deciding.

items.stem: Leadership wants a delivery date for a six-month project with many unknowns. What do you give them?
choices: Your guess tripled, presented as the date
A range with your confidence, broken into milestones, with the biggest unknowns tackled first, and an updated range as you learn
No estimate until everything is known
One optimistic date
why: Hidden padding erodes trust when it's discovered.
A range is honest about uncertainty, milestones show progress, and tackling unknowns early narrows the range fastest.
Leadership still has to plan; refusing helps no one.
Almost certain to slip, and trust goes with it.

items.stem: An engineer has underperformed for months despite clear feedback. What's the right next step?
choices: Set out specific, measurable expectations in writing with support and a clear timeline, review progress regularly, and involve HR so the process is fair
Quietly move them to another team
Let them go without warning
Keep tolerating it
why: Clear expectations give them a real chance to improve, and a documented, fair process protects them and the team whatever the outcome.
Moves the problem, and it isn't fair to them or the other team.
Unfair, and risky for the company.
The team carries the cost and resents it.
